title: Paloma and the Portrait
premise: Wendell Thackeray, the unassuming coroner of Marrow Creek, has spent years quietly proving that three 'accidental' deaths were murders, all connected to the town's founding family, the Ashcombes. When a confession letter arrives postmarked the day after the fourth victim's funeral, Wendell realizes someone is watching him—and wants him to find a ledger hidden in a portrait at Ashcombe Hall that names every bribe, every cover-up, and every killer. As the annual Founders' Anniversary Dinner approaches, Wendell must decode the ledger before the family destroys it and silences him too. The story ends when Wendell exposes the ledger publicly at the dinner itself, trading his invisibility for justice as the true killer—the family matriarch's devoted archivist—is arrested.
about_author: Wren Amberdale is the pen name of a former small-town newspaper reporter who covered coroner's inquests for eleven years before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries about quiet people who notice what others bury.

chapters.title: The Man Who Knew Every Grave
chapters.summary: Wendell Thackeray walks the cemetery at dawn, cataloging headstones and reflecting on the three deaths he quietly proved were murders—deaths the police ruled accidents. His POV establishes his methodical mind and deliberate invisibility. Emotional beat: lonely competence, the comfort of being overlooked.

chapters.title: A Fourth Accident
chapters.summary: Harlan Ashcombe, youngest son of the founding family, drowns in two feet of creek water. Wendell examines the body and finds ligature marks the sheriff refuses to see. Through Wendell's eyes, we feel the old pattern reasserting itself. Emotional beat: dread wrapped in professional calm.

chapters.title: The Letter Postmarked Too Late
chapters.summary: Three days after Harlan's funeral, a confession letter arrives at Wendell's office—postmarked the day after the funeral, unsigned, referencing details only the killer would know. It mentions 'the portrait keeps the count.' Wendell realizes he's being invited into the game. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: Ashcombe Hall
chapters.summary: Wendell attends the funeral reception under pretense of condolence, surveying Ashcombe Hall: its portraits, its matriarch Vivienne, her cold son Edmund, and the soft-spoken archivist Milo Fenwick who watches Wendell too closely. Third-person limited on Wendell. Emotional beat: the hunter realizing he may be prey.

chapters.title: What the Dead Keep
chapters.summary: Wendell reopens his private files on the three earlier deaths—a fall from the mill catwalk, a barn fire, a 'heart attack'—and maps them against Ashcombe business dealings. Each victim had threatened to talk. Emotional beat: grief for victims no one else mourns correctly.

chapters.title: The Sheriff's Warning
chapters.summary: Sheriff Dale Pruitt, whose campaigns were funded by Ashcombe money, warns Wendell off over coffee: 'Some graves you dig for other people.' Wendell understands the corruption reaches the law itself. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; justice must come from outside the system.

chapters.title: Portrait of a Founder
chapters.summary: Wendell studies photographs of the Hall's centerpiece portrait of Ezekiel Ashcombe and notices faint grid marks beneath the varnish—canvas scored in ledger-like columns. The confession letter's phrase clicks: the portrait literally keeps count. Emotional beat: electric discovery tempered by caution.

chapters.title: Milo Fenwick's Quiet Eyes
chapters.summary: Wendell probes the archivist, who deflects with charm but lets slip knowledge of the second victim's last appointment. A chapter from Milo's own POV reveals he is cataloging everything—for reasons he tells himself are loyalty. Emotional beat: ambiguity; is Milo ally, killer, or both?

chapters.title: Vivienne's Toast
chapters.summary: At a charity gala, matriarch Vivienne Ashcombe delivers a toast honoring Harlan, and Wendell watches her hands tremble on the glass—not with grief, he suspects, but with the strain of holding a family together by any means. Emotional beat: recognizing power as performance.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: Another letter arrives, this one containing a torn corner of canvas and a date: the anniversary dinner, three weeks away. The writer taunts Wendell's slowness. He realizes the letters began only after he started asking questions—someone inside the house is steering him. Emotional beat: paranoia braided with resolve.

chapters.title: Ledger in Plain Sight
chapters.summary: Wendell consults a retired art restorer, Ida Kroll, who confirms the portrait was painted over an older work—likely a genuine account book rendered in paint, a founder's insurance against his own heirs. Emotional beat: wonder at how secrets hide in what everyone sees daily.

chapters.title: Breaking Into the Past
chapters.summary: Wendell and Ida photograph the portrait during a public open house, but Edmund Ashcombe catches them and has Wendell escorted out with a threat dressed as courtesy. Emotional beat: humiliation curdling into defiance; the stakes are now personal.

chapters.title: The Mill Catwalk Again
chapters.summary: Wendell returns to the site of the first death and finds evidence someone recently searched it—fresh scuffs, a dropped cufflink monogrammed M.F. Milo was there first. Wendell can no longer tell if Milo is hunting the truth or erasing witnesses to it. Emotional beat: trust collapsing.

chapters.title: Decoding Ezekiel
chapters.summary: Ida's infrared images reveal columns of figures keyed to dates and initials. Wendell cross-references with parish records and land deeds, reconstructing a century of payments—bribes, hush money, and four entries marked with a small painted skull. Emotional beat: grim awe at inherited rot.

chapters.title: Four Skulls, Four Names
chapters.summary: The skull-marked entries correspond exactly to Wendell's three old cases plus Harlan. But the final entry is dated next month—the anniversary dinner—with initials W.T. The ledger predicts his death. Emotional beat: cold terror met with stubborn refusal to run.

chapters.title: An Offer from the House
chapters.summary: Edmund offers Wendell a paid position as 'historical consultant,' a gilded muzzle. Wendell declines, and that night his office is ransacked—his files taken, the letters left behind as a message. Emotional beat: the cost of visibility made real.

chapters.title: The Confession Behind the Confession
chapters.summary: Wendell traps the letter-writer using a false detail only he planted: Milo Fenwick responds to it, revealing himself—but not as Harlan's killer. Milo confesses he witnessed Vivienne order Harlan's death and has been feeding Wendell clues because the law will never touch her. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance, guilt shared.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Burden
chapters.summary: Milo's full account: forty years serving the family, complicit in silence, finally broken by Harlan's murder. He cannot testify without destroying himself, so he built the letter campaign to make Wendell the instrument. Emotional beat: moral compromise examined; justice needs dirty hands.

chapters.title: Anniversary Eve
chapters.summary: On the eve of the dinner, Vivienne orders the portrait removed for 'restoration'—actually destruction. Milo alerts Wendell; they plan to swap the canvas with a replica Ida paints overnight. Emotional beat: breathless preparation, the sense of one chance.

chapters.title: The Glass Raised
chapters.summary: At the anniversary dinner, as Vivienne raises her toast, Wendell stands and reads aloud the decoded ledger entries—dates, sums, and the four skull-marked deaths—to a room of stunned townspeople. Edmund lunges; the sheriff, cornered by witnesses, must act. Emotional beat: cathartic exposure, courage at last visible.

chapters.title: What Justice Costs
chapters.summary: In the aftermath, Vivienne is charged, Edmund flees, and Milo surrenders to perjury charges willingly, calling it fair payment. Wendell testifies, ending his career as invisible man but gaining something harder: a town that now watches him. Emotional beat: bittersweet vindication.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Months later, Wendell adds proper markers to the three forgotten victims and visits Harlan's grave. The restored portrait hangs in the county courthouse, ledger legible to all. He still walks the cemetery at dawn—but no longer alone; Ida walks beside him. Emotional beat: peace earned, memory honored.
